messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rohan's eyes scanned the courtroom with a practiced air of authority, his years as a judge having honed his ability to remain composed under pressure. Yet, despite his professional demeanor, the 31-year-old's life had been forever altered by the natural disaster that struck his hometown five years ago. The devastating hurricane had left an indelible mark on Rohan, one that he struggled to keep at bay. It started with the sounds of ambulances racing down the streets outside his courthouse window. The sirens would transport him back to the chaotic days following the hurricane, when rescue teams combed through the rubble in search of survivors. The smell of antiseptic wafting from the hospital across the street was another potent trigger, instantly conjuring images of makeshift medical tents and the countless injured people he had seen. Rohan's mind would begin to reel as he associated these sights and smells with the traumatic event, his thoughts spiraling into a vortex of anxiety. In an attempt to stave off these debilitating memories, Rohan developed a series of maladaptive strategies. He found himself avoiding relaxation at all costs, believing that letting his guard down would render him vulnerable to the flashbacks that haunted him. He would suppress thoughts of the hurricane, forcing them deep into his subconscious whenever they threatened to surface. Going out in public became an ordeal; Rohan was convinced that every weather forecast might herald a repeat disaster. As he navigated these landmines, his avoidance behaviors grew more pronounced. When memories did break through Rohan's defenses, they arrived with jarring intensity. He would relive the traumatic experience across all his senses at once – the howling wind, the stench of saltwater and mud, the anguished cries for help. These sensory snapshots were seared into his brain like photographs, each one a discrete, terrifying moment in time. Visual memories dominated Rohan's recollections: images of splintered buildings, uprooted trees, and ravaged streets that had once been familiar. The more these memories resurfaced, the greater his need to suppress them – and so the cycle repeated itself. As Rohan's avoidance behaviors became more entrenched, they in turn triggered fresh waves of anxiety. His life began to contract, with social engagements and even routine outings curtailed by the fear of encountering something that might set off a flashback. His wife grew concerned about his increasingly withdrawn nature, though Rohan struggled to articulate the root causes of his distress. The strain was beginning to tell on Rohan's professional life as well. As a judge, he prided himself on remaining impartial and composed under pressure – but now found himself avoiding cases involving natural disasters or emergency responders. His usual acuity began to falter, as if his mind was perpetually elsewhere, bracing for the next trigger. It was this creeping sense of disintegration that finally prompted Rohan to seek help. Fearing he might lose himself entirely in the undertow of his memories, he made an appointment with a therapist – hoping against hope that she could guide him toward some measure of peace.
